items.prompt: A rule written LAST in the stylesheet doesn't apply — an older rule wins instead. What are the three factors the cascade checks, and in what order?
choices: Source order only — the browser never looks at anything else
Origin & importance first, then specificity, then source order as the final tiebreaker
Specificity first, then origin & importance, then source order
File size of the stylesheet, then alphabetical selector name, then source order
items.explanation: The cascade checks origin/importance first (is anything !important, or from a different source), then specificity, and only falls back to source order once both of those are tied. Source order being written last never overrides a stronger specificity.
items.reference:
1. Origin & importance
2. Specificity
3. Source order (last resort)

Why: each step only gets consulted if every earlier step is a dead tie.
items.learnMore:
The cascade's real priority chain

Most CSS debugging confusion comes from assuming source order decides everything. It's actually the LAST of three checks — origin/importance and specificity both get a chance to decide the winner first.

Common mistake

Moving a rule further down the file to 'fix' it, without checking whether specificity already decided the outcome.

choices: Rule B — later in the file always wins
Rule A — specificity is checked before source order, so being written later doesn't matter
Whichever one has a shorter selector
It's undefined behavior and depends on the browser
items.explanation: Source order is only the tiebreaker used when specificity (and origin/importance) are tied. Higher specificity wins regardless of position in the file.

2. Specificity
3. Source order (last resort)

items.prompt: `#page .toolbar .btn` (1 id, 2 classes) competes with `.btn-primary` (1 class). Which wins?
choices: `.btn-primary` — it's shorter, and shorter selectors are more specific
`#page .toolbar .btn` — its id alone outranks any number of classes
They tie, so source order decides
Neither applies, since they conflict
items.explanation: Specificity compares ids first. `#page .toolbar .btn` has 1 id, `.btn-primary` has 0 — the id column alone decides it, before class counts are even compared.
items.reference:
Selector(id, class, elem)Beats
#page .toolbar .btn(1, 2, 0).btn-primary (0,1,0) — id column decides
button.btn(0, 1, 1).btn-primary (0,1,0) — element column breaks the tie
inline style=""beats all (origin)#page (1,0,0) and everything else

Why: compare id, then class, then element — no carrying between columns; origin (inline styles) is checked before specificity at all.
items.learnMore:
No carrying between columns

Specificity compares (ids, classes, elements) left to right, like an odometer with no carrying. A single id always beats any number of classes, because the comparison stops at the first differing column.

Common mistake

Thinking 'shorter selector = wins' or 'more words = wins' — length has nothing to do with it, only the id/class/element counts do.

items.prompt: `button.btn` (0 ids, 1 class, 1 element) competes with `.btn-primary` (0 ids, 1 class, 0 elements). Which wins?

`button.btn` — ids tie at 0, classes tie at 1, so the element column breaks the tie in its favor
They're exactly equal, so it's a coin flip
`.btn-primary`, because pseudo-classes always outrank type selectors
items.explanation: When ids and classes both tie, the element column becomes the deciding factor. button.btn has 1 element (button) where .btn-primary has 0, so button.btn wins.

A `

items.explanation: Inheritance is a different mechanism from the cascade: some properties (color, font-family) pass down from parent to child by default. The cascade resolves conflicts between competing rules; inheritance fills in values when there's no competing rule at all.

Inherits by defaultDoes NOT inherit

Why: inheritance and the cascade are separate mechanisms that happen to interact.
items.learnMore:
Inheritance vs. cascade

The cascade decides which competing DECLARATION wins for a given element and property. Inheritance is what happens when there's no declaration at all for a property on an element — some properties fall back to the parent's computed value, others fall back to a fixed initial value instead.

Common mistake

Assuming a border or padding will 'inherit' from a parent the way color does — border and padding never inherit by default.

items.prompt: A developer sets `border: 1px solid red` on a parent `<div>` and expects every nested `<span>` to also have that border, the way `color` would pass down. What actually happens?

Nothing — `border` doesn't inherit by default, so nested spans get no border unless a rule targets them directly
Only the color of the border inherits, not the width
It depends on whether the span has a class
items.explanation: border does not inherit by default — unlike color, font-family, or line-height, it falls back to its own initial value (none) rather than the parent's computed value.

items.prompt: A developer adds `!important` to win a specificity fight. What's the real cost of doing this?
choices: There is no cost — `!important` is a clean, permanent fix
It escalates the conflict rather than resolving it — only another `!important` declaration can override it later, often starting an arms race
It only works in some browsers, so it's unreliable
It automatically removes the competing rule from the stylesheet
items.explanation: !important jumps to the front of the origin-and-importance check, ahead of specificity. The only thing that can beat it later is another !important rule that wins among !important declarations — which routinely triggers an escalating arms race of !important on both sides.
items.reference:
!important wins the battle

...but only another !important can win the NEXT battle against it.

Why: !important opts a declaration out of ordinary specificity comparison entirely.
items.learnMore:
Why !important compounds

Once one team reaches for !important, any future override of that rule also needs !important — and once two competing !important rules exist, THEIR conflict resolves by specificity among just the !important ones. Each use makes the next override harder, not easier.

Common mistake

Treating !important as a permanent fix rather than a debt that the next person has to pay off with another !important.

items.prompt: A rule is marked `!important`. A later rule with much higher specificity (but no `!important`) tries to override it. What happens?
choices: The higher-specificity rule wins, because specificity always wins
The `!important` rule still wins — origin & importance is checked before specificity, regardless of how specific the competing selector is
They average their values
The later rule wins because it comes after in the file
items.explanation: Specificity is only compared among rules that are already tied on origin & importance. A plain (non-important) rule, no matter how specific its selector, cannot beat an !important rule.
items.reference:
!important wins the battle

...but only another !important can win the NEXT battle against it.

Why: !important opts a declaration out of ordinary specificity comparison entirely.

items.prompt: What is the specificity tuple `(ids, classes, elements)` for the selector `.card .title`?
items.explanation: .card and .title are both classes — no ids, no element/type selectors — giving (0, 2, 0).
items.reference:
.card .title→ (0, 2, 0)
div p a:hover→ (0, 1, 3)

Why: count each id/class/element token in the selector, left to right — :hover is a pseudo-CLASS (single colon), so it lands in the class column, not the element column.
items.learnMore:
Computing a tuple by hand

Walk the selector left to right and tally: '#' tokens go in the id column, '.' / '[attr]' / single-colon pseudo-classes go in the class column, bare tag names and '::' pseudo-elements go in the element column.

Common mistake

Counting the number of words in the selector instead of the number of id/class/element tokens.

div p a:hover→ (0, 1, 3)

items.prompt: `.btn { color: red }` and `.btn { color: blue }` both appear in the same stylesheet, targeting the same element, with identical specificity. Which color renders?
choices: Red — the first one always wins ties
Blue — the later declaration wins when specificity and origin/importance are both tied
An average/blend of the two colors
Neither — the browser rejects the conflicting rule
items.explanation: With identical specificity and no !important on either side, source order is the tiebreaker — the later declaration wins.
items.reference:
.btn { color: red } ← written first

.btn { color: blue } ← written later, WINS

Why: identical specificity means source order is the only thing left to decide it.
items.learnMore:
When source order actually matters

Source order is a real, correct tiebreaker — it's just the LAST one checked, not the first. When two selectors are structurally identical (or coincidentally produce the same tuple), the later one in the cascade wins.

Common mistake

Generalizing 'the later rule won here' into 'source order always decides' — it only decided because specificity was tied.

items.prompt: Put the cascade's tiebreak steps in the correct order: [specificity, source order, origin & importance].
choices: Origin & importance → specificity → source order
Source order → specificity → origin & importance
Specificity → origin & importance → source order
All three are checked simultaneously and averaged
items.explanation: The chain is origin & importance first (browser default < user < author, with !important flipping priority), then specificity, then source order as the final tiebreak.
items.reference:
1. Origin & importance
2. Specificity (id, class, element tuple)
3. Source order

Why: each step is a tiebreak for the step before it — it only runs if the earlier step is exactly tied.
items.learnMore:
The full chain, precisely

Origin & importance covers where the rule came from (browser default, user stylesheet, author stylesheet) and whether it's marked !important, which flips the normal origin priority. Only once that's tied does specificity get compared; only once THAT'S tied does source order decide.

Common mistake

Memorizing the steps but applying them out of order when actually debugging — checking source order first out of habit.

items.prompt: Why does the cascade check origin & importance BEFORE specificity, rather than after?
choices: It's an arbitrary implementation detail with no real reason
So that things like user-defined accessibility stylesheets or !important overrides can reliably override author CSS no matter how specific the author's selectors are
Because origin is cheaper for the browser to compute than specificity
It doesn't — specificity is actually checked first
items.explanation: Checking origin/importance first means a user's accessibility stylesheet (or an !important override) can guarantee it wins regardless of how specific the page author's CSS is — if specificity were checked first, an author could always out-specify a user override.

2. Specificity (id, class, element tuple)
3. Source order

items.prompt: Why is specificity described as a tuple compared 'with no carrying between columns' instead of a single additive score?
choices: Because it makes the math harder for no reason
Because if it were additive, enough classes could eventually outweigh an id — tuple comparison guarantees an id always wins regardless of how many classes the other selector has
It isn't a tuple — that's a common misconception
Because browsers can't do addition efficiently
items.explanation: Tuple (not additive) comparison is what guarantees a single id always outranks any number of classes — the id column is compared first, and if it differs, the comparison stops right there.
items.reference:
Model11 classes vs. 1 id
Additive (wrong)11×10=110 > 100 → classes 'win'
Tuple (correct)(0,11,0) vs (1,0,0) → id wins

Why: the id column is compared first and decides it outright.
items.learnMore:
The additive model breaks down

The id=100/class=10/element=1 shorthand is a fine mental model for small, everyday comparisons, but it's not literally what browsers compute — real comparison is componentwise, so no number of classes ever outweighs a single id.

Common mistake

Multiplying out the additive shorthand for selectors with 10+ classes and getting the wrong answer as a result.

items.prompt: Selector A has tuple (0, 3, 5). Selector B has tuple (0, 3, 2). Which wins, and on which column does the comparison actually resolve?
choices: A wins, resolved on the id column
A wins, resolved on the element column (ids tie at 0, classes tie at 3, elements differ 5 vs 2)
B wins, because fewer elements means a more targeted selector
They tie, since both have 0 ids
items.explanation: Ids tie (0=0), classes tie (3=3), so the comparison proceeds to the element column, where 5 > 2 — A wins there.

No — classes are compared before elements, so a single class beats any number of elements, no matter how many
Only in Chrome

items.prompt: `@layer legacy, components;` declares two layers. A rule in `legacy` has specificity (1, 2, 0). A rule in `components` has specificity (0, 1, 0). Which wins?
choices: `legacy`'s rule — higher specificity always wins regardless of layers
`components`'s rule — layer order is checked before specificity, and `components` was declared as the later (higher-priority) layer
They tie and source order decides
Layers only affect load order, not which rule applies
items.explanation: @layer inserts a new priority check BEFORE specificity: a later-declared layer beats an earlier one regardless of specificity (as long as neither is !important). components was declared second, so it wins even with lower specificity.
items.reference:
@layer legacy, components;

components (declared later) beats legacy — regardless of specificity

Why: layer priority is checked before specificity in the cascade.
items.learnMore:
@layer changes the chain

Normally: origin/importance → specificity → order. With layers involved: origin/importance → LAYER ORDER → specificity (within the same layer) → source order. A later layer beats an earlier layer outright, no matter how specific the earlier layer's selectors are.

Common mistake

Forgetting that UNLAYERED css always beats any layered css (except !important) — layering only your new CSS won't help against unlayered legacy CSS.

items.prompt: A rule sits outside any `@layer` block (unlayered). Another rule sits inside `@layer components`. Both target the same element/property, neither is `!important`. Which wins?
choices: The unlayered rule always wins, regardless of specificity — unlayered CSS has the highest layer priority by spec
The layered rule always wins, since layers were explicitly declared
Whichever has higher specificity, ignoring layers entirely
It's undefined and varies by browser
items.explanation: Per spec, unlayered CSS has higher priority than any declared layer. This is why wrapping only your NEW css in a layer doesn't help against old, unlayered legacy CSS — the legacy CSS would still win.
items.reference:
@layer legacy, components;

components (declared later) beats legacy — regardless of specificity

Why: layer priority is checked before specificity in the cascade.

items.prompt: `:where(#app .toolbar) .btn` matches the same elements as `#app .toolbar .btn`. What's its specificity?
choices: (1, 1, 0) — the id and outer class still count
(0, 1, 0) — everything inside :where() contributes zero specificity, only `.btn` outside it counts
(0, 0, 0) — :where() zeroes out the entire selector, including .btn
Identical to #app .toolbar .btn — :where() only affects matching, not specificity
items.explanation: :where()'s contents (here, #app .toolbar) contribute zero specificity by spec, regardless of what's inside. Only the part outside :where() — .btn — counts, giving (0, 1, 0).
items.reference:
:where(#app .toolbar) .btn

→ (0, 1, 0) — only .btn (outside :where()) counts

Why: :where()'s ENTIRE argument list contributes zero specificity, by spec.
items.learnMore:
:where() vs. :is()

:where() and :is() match identically, but :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument, while :where() always contributes zero. This makes :where() the right tool specifically for 'match this, but don't let it out-compete anything.'

Common mistake

Reaching for :is() when the goal is actually to LOWER specificity — :is() doesn't lower it, :where() does.

items.prompt: Why would a team wrap a legacy selector in `:where(...)` instead of just deleting the legacy rule outright?
choices: It's purely cosmetic and has no functional effect

It keeps the legacy rule matching (and still applying where nothing overrides it) while making it trivially easy for any new rule to override, without risking removing styles something else still depends on
It makes the legacy rule apply with higher priority than before
It's required syntax and has no alternative
items.explanation: :where() keeps the legacy selector functionally matching (so nothing relying on it breaks), but drops its specificity to near-zero, so any reasonable new rule can override it — safer than deleting outright, which risks removing a style something else still needs.
items.reference:
:where(#app .toolbar) .btn

→ (0, 1, 0) — only .btn (outside :where()) counts

Why: :where()'s ENTIRE argument list contributes zero specificity, by spec.

:where() and :is() match identically, but :is() takes the specificity of its most specific argument, while :where() always contributes zero. This makes :where() the right tool specifically for 'match this, but don't let it out-compete anything.'

Common mistake

Reaching for :is() when the goal is actually to LOWER specificity — :is() doesn't lower it, :where() does.

items.prompt: Why do utility-first (Tailwind-style) and BEM codebases rarely develop 'specificity wars,' while codebases with deep id-based nesting often do?
choices: Utility/BEM classes are shorter strings, and shorter strings have lower specificity
Utility/BEM rules almost always target an element with a single class — (0,1,0) regardless of DOM nesting — while id-based nesting accumulates specificity as the DOM gets deeper
Utility-first frameworks disable the cascade entirely
BEM and utility-first are functionally identical to id-based nesting in specificity terms
items.explanation: Utility and BEM rules target a single class per rule, keeping specificity flat at (0,1,0) no matter how deep the DOM nesting is. Id-based nesting like `#page .toolbar .btn` accumulates specificity as more ancestor structure gets baked into the selector.
items.reference:
StyleTypical tuple
Utility-first / BEM(0, 1, 0) — flat
Legacy id-nestingGrows with DOM depth

Why: flat specificity means conflicts resolve predictably by source order instead of an escalating fight.
items.learnMore:
Predictability as a design goal

A methodology that keeps specificity flat trades some selector expressiveness for predictability: when two rules conflict, you already know it'll resolve by source order, not by an id-vs-class arms race that requires memorizing the whole file's history.

Common mistake

Adding a single id selector 'just this once' into an otherwise flat-specificity codebase — it immediately breaks the predictability the rest of the codebase relies on.

items.prompt: A legacy codebase's selectors keep growing more specific over time (more ids, deeper nesting) even though the team never intended that. What's driving the growth?
choices: Random chance — specificity naturally drifts upward over time with no cause
Selectors are typically written by following the DOM's ancestor structure, so as the DOM nests deeper, the selectors needed to target something precisely nest deeper too, accumulating specificity
CSS files automatically increase specificity with each save
Browser updates periodically raise the specificity of existing selectors
items.explanation: When selectors are written by following DOM structure (rather than a flat class-per-component convention), deeper nesting naturally produces more specific selectors — each additional ancestor in the selector adds to the tuple.

items.prompt: A legacy rule inside `@layer legacy` uses `!important`. A new rule inside the later-declared `@layer components` does not. Which wins?
choices: `components` — later layers always win
`legacy` — !important is checked at the origin & importance step, which happens BEFORE layer order is even considered
They tie and source order decides
Neither applies, and the property falls back to its initial value
items.explanation: Neither :where() nor @layer changes the outcome against an !important declaration — origin & importance is checked before layer order or specificity, so an !important rule in an earlier layer still wins over a normal rule in a later layer.
items.reference:
!important beats layers too

Layer order and :where() only affect steps that run AFTER origin & importance.

Why: !important is resolved before layer priority is even consulted.
items.learnMore:
!important as the true top of the chain

Of everything covered in this unit — specificity, source order, :where(), @layer — only origin & importance sits above all of them. An !important declaration is unaffected by lowering specificity with :where() or reordering layers with @layer.

Common mistake

Trying to fix an !important conflict with @layer reordering alone — it won't work; the fix has to remove or match the !important itself.

items.prompt: Implement `calculateSpecificity(parts)`. `parts` is an array of selector tokens (e.g. `['#app', '.toolbar', '.btn']`). Return `{ ids, classes, elements }` where: a token starting with `#` is an id; a token starting with `::` is a (pseudo-)element; a token starting with `.`, `[`, or `:` (single colon) is a class/attribute/pseudo-class; anything else (a bare tag name) is an element.

tests.expr: expect(calculateSpecificity(['#app', '.toolbar', '.btn'])).toEqual({ ids: 1, classes: 2, elements: 0 })

expect(calculateSpecificity(['button', '.btn'])).toEqual({ ids: 0, classes: 1, elements: 1 })

items.explanation: This mirrors the real specificity tuple from L3's incident: walk the tokens, bucket each into ids/classes/elements by its leading character, checking '::' before ':' so pseudo-elements don't get miscounted as pseudo-classes.

items.prompt: Implement `calculateSpecificity(parts)` (same rules as before: `#`→id, `::`→element, `.`/`[`/single `:`→class, bare word→element). Verify it correctly handles an attribute selector and a pseudo-element.

expect(calculateSpecificity([])).toEqual({ ids: 0, classes: 0, elements: 0 })

items.explanation: Attribute selectors ([href]) count as classes per spec, same weight as a class or single-colon pseudo-class. Pseudo-elements (::before) count as elements — checking the '::' prefix before the single ':' prefix is what keeps these from being miscounted.

items.prompt: Implement `calculateSpecificity(parts)` (same rules). Confirm it reproduces the exact tuple for `button.btn` from this unit's tables.

items.explanation: Reproducing the unit's own worked examples with real code is the point — this is the exact function a specificity linter runs, just simplified to take pre-split tokens instead of parsing a raw selector string.

items.prompt: Implement `compareSpecificity(a, b)` where `a` and `b` are `{ ids, classes, elements }` tuples. Return a positive number if `a` wins, negative if `b` wins, 0 if tied — compare ids first, then classes, then elements, with no carrying between columns.

tests.expr: expect(compareSpecificity({ ids: 1, classes: 0, elements: 0 }, { ids: 0, classes: 10, elements: 10 }) > 0).toBeTruthy()

tests.description: tie on ids and classes, elements break it

expect(compareSpecificity({ ids: 0, classes: 1, elements: 0 }, { ids: 0, classes: 1, elements: 0 })).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Comparing ids first (returning immediately if they differ) is what implements 'no carrying' — a difference in an earlier column short-circuits the whole comparison before later columns are even inspected.

items.explanation: This is the same comparison the browser effectively runs — reproducing the incident's outcome in code confirms the mental model of the cascade matches what actually happened in production.

items.prompt: Implement `compareSpecificity(a, b)` (same semantics). Verify the odometer property: a tuple with more elements never beats one with fewer classes.

tests.expr: expect(compareSpecificity({ ids: 0, classes: 0, elements: 50 }, { ids: 0, classes: 1, elements: 0 }) < 0).toBeTruthy()

tests.expr: expect(compareSpecificity({ ids: 1, classes: 0, elements: 0 }, { ids: 0, classes: 99, elements: 99 }) > 0).toBeTruthy()

items.explanation: Because ids and classes are checked before elements, and each check short-circuits on any difference, no amount of elements can compensate for fewer classes, and no amount of classes can compensate for fewer ids.

items.prompt: Implement `resolveWinner(declarations)`, returning the INDEX of the winning declaration. Each declaration is `{ parts, order, important }`. Rule: if any declaration is `important`, only compare among the important ones; otherwise compare all. Among the candidates, highest specificity (using `calculateSpecificity`/`compareSpecificity` from earlier) wins; ties break by highest `order` (later wins). Assume `calculateSpecificity` and `compareSpecificity` are already defined and available.

tests.description: higher specificity wins over later source order
tests.expr: expect(resolveWinner([{ parts: ['#app', '.toolbar', '.btn'], order: 1, important: false }, { parts: ['.ds-button--primary'], order: 2, important: false }])).toBe(0)

tests.expr: expect(resolveWinner([{ parts: ['.btn'], order: 1, important: false }, { parts: ['.btn'], order: 2, important: false }])).toBe(1)
expect(resolveWinner([{ parts: ['#app', '.btn'], order: 1, important: false }, { parts: ['.btn'], order: 2, important: true }])).toBe(1)

items.explanation: This is the whole three-step chain (origin/importance → specificity → order) implemented directly: filter to important declarations if any exist, then fold over the remaining pool comparing specificity first and order only as the tiebreak — exactly mirroring the cascade's own priority chain from L2.

items.prompt: Implement `resolveWinner(declarations)` (same semantics as before). Verify it correctly picks the LATER of two declarations when both specificity and importance tie exactly.

items.explanation: With three equally-specific single-class selectors, order is the only differentiator left — the fold correctly keeps replacing `best` whenever a later-order declaration ties on specificity, landing on the highest order among the tied group.

items.prompt: Implement `resolveLayerWinner(layerOrder, declA, declB)`. `layerOrder` is an array of layer names in declared order (later index = higher priority). `declA`/`declB` are `{ layer, important }` — `layer` may be `null` for unlayered CSS. items.explanation: This encodes the exact priority chain from L2/L3: important beats everything, unlayered beats any declared layer, and among declared layers the later-declared one wins — matching how @layer inserts a check before ordinary specificity.
